1. R22 VCR cycle with superheat and subcooling: 2024 1(c) and 2021 1(c)

Topic A4 · 13 + 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

A refrigeration system using R22 is to have a refrigerating capacity of 80 kW. The system follows a VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) cycle with 5 °C subcooling and 10 °C superheating, in which the evaporating and condensing temperatures are −10 °C and 45 °C. Determine: (i) the volume flow rate of refrigerant, (ii) COP, (iii) the power required to drive the compressor. (Same question word for word in 2021 1(c), 15 marks.)

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Where things happen. Superheating happens at the end of the evaporator: the refrigerant finishes boiling at −10 °C, then warms 10 K more, to 0 °C, while still at evaporator pressure. Subcooling happens at the end of the condenser: the vapour finishes condensing at 45 °C, then the liquid cools 5 K more, to 40 °C, while still at condenser pressure.

PointWhereStateFound on the P–h chart as the crossing of
1leaving evaporator, entering compressorsuperheated vapour, 0 °Chorizontal line pe (sat. pressure at −10 °C) × isotherm 0 °C (right of dome)
2leaving compressorsuperheated vapour, about 81 °Chorizontal line pc (sat. pressure at 45 °C) × constant-s line through 1
3leaving condensersubcooled liquid, 40 °Chorizontal line pc × isotherm 40 °C (vertical, left of dome) ≈ hf at 40 °C
4leaving expansion valvewet mixture at −10 °Cvertical line down from 3 (h4 = h3) × horizontal line pe

Why h3 = hf(40 °C)? Liquid enthalpy hardly depends on pressure, so subcooled liquid at 40 °C has (almost) the same h as saturated liquid at 40 °C. That is the standard textbook step.

What you need: h1, h2, h3 (= h4) and v1. Everything else is arithmetic: RE (refrigerating effect) = h1 − h4, w = h2 − h1, m = Q/RE, V = m v1.

D. UNDERSTANDProperty-table rows used (how to read the table)

Table basis (Moran A-7, A-9; h = 0 at −40 °C liquid)

pe = 3.5485 bar, pc = 17.298 bar [A-7]

State 1 (3.5485 bar, 0 °C): fraction = (3.5485 − 3.5)/(4.0 − 3.5) = 0.097
h1 = 253.21 + 0.097(252.14 − 253.21) = 253.11
s1 = 0.9700 + 0.097(0.9542 − 0.9700) = 0.9685
v1 = 0.06956 + 0.097(0.06011 − 0.06956) = 0.0686 m³/kg [A-9]

State 2 (s = 0.9685):
16 bar: h = 287.30 + 0.687(295.93 − 287.30) = 293.23
18 bar: h = 293.40 + 0.368(302.16 − 293.40) = 296.62
at 17.298 bar: h2 = 293.23 + 0.649(296.62 − 293.23) = 295.43 [A-9]

State 3: h3 = hf(40 °C) = 94.53 [A-7]

RE = h1 − h4 = 253.11 − 94.53 = 158.58 kJ/kg
w = h2 − h1 = 295.43 − 253.11 = 42.32 kJ/kg
COP = RE / w = 158.58 / 42.32 = 3.75
m = Q / RE = 80 / 158.58 = 0.5045 kg/s
V = m v1 = 0.5045 × 0.0686 = 0.0346 m³/s
P = m w = 0.5045 × 42.32 = 21.35 kW

Chart basis (R22 P–h chart, IIR: h = 200 at 0 °C liquid)

pe = 3.55 bar, pc = 17.29 bar [chart]

State 1: read at 3.55 bar × 0 °C
h1 = 408.2, s1 = 1.792, v1 = 0.0686 m³/kg [chart]

State 2: follow s = 1.792 up to 17.29 bar
h2 = 450.4 (t2 ≈ 81 °C) [chart]

State 3: h3 = hf(40 °C) = 249.6 [chart]

RE = h1 − h4 = 408.2 − 249.6 = 158.6 kJ/kg
w = h2 − h1 = 450.4 − 408.2 = 42.2 kJ/kg
COP = RE / w = 158.6 / 42.2 = 3.76
m = Q / RE = 80 / 158.6 = 0.5044 kg/s
V = m v1 = 0.5044 × 0.0686 = 0.0346 m³/s
P = m w = 0.5044 × 42.2 = 21.29 kW

All h values here are about 155.1 kJ/kg higher than the table column: only the zero is different.

Same answers on both sides: RE ≈ 158.6, w ≈ 42.2–42.3, COP ≈ 3.75, m ≈ 0.5045 kg/s, V ≈ 0.0346 m³/s, P ≈ 21.3 kW. Use one column only.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: R22, Q = 80 kW, te = −10 °C, tc = 45 °C, superheat 10 K, subcool 5 K.

State points (from R22 P–h chart):

Statep (bar)t (°C)h (kJ/kg)Source
1 (superheated vapour)3.550408.2; v1 = 0.0686 m³/kgchart
2 (after isentropic compression)17.29≈ 81450.4chart, s2 = s1
3 (subcooled liquid)17.2940249.6chart, hf at 40 °C
4 (after throttling)3.55−10249.6h4 = h3

Refrigerating effect, RE = h1 − h4 = 408.2 − 249.6 = 158.6 kJ/kg

Compressor work, w = h2 − h1 = 450.4 − 408.2 = 42.2 kJ/kg

Mass flow, m = Q / RE = 80 / 158.6 = 0.5044 kg/s

(i) Volume flow rate (at compressor suction), V = m v1 = 0.5044 × 0.0686 = 0.0346 m³/s

(ii) COP = RE / w = 158.6 / 42.2 = 3.76

(iii) Power, P = m w = 0.5044 × 42.2 = 21.3 kW

P–h sketch checklist (draw it, 2 marks):

  1. Saturation dome; two horizontal lines: pc (top) and pe (bottom).
  2. Point 1 on the pe line, right of the saturated-vapour curve (superheated).
  3. 1→2 along a constant-s line up to pc.
  4. Point 3 on the pc line, left of the saturated-liquid curve (subcooled).
  5. 3→4 vertical (h4 = h3) down to pe. Label h1, h2, h3 on the h-axis.

If the exam gives Tables A-7/A-9 instead of the chart, write the left column of section D in the same table form: h1 = 253.11, h2 = 295.43, h3 = 94.53, v1 = 0.0686. Answers come out the same.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Mixing tables with different h zeros. h1 from the chart (408) with h3 from Table A-7 (94.5) gives RE = 314: wrong by double. Take every h from one source.
  • Volume flow at the wrong point. “Volume flow rate of refrigerant” means at compressor suction, so use v1 (0.0686), not v at 2 or vg at −10 °C (0.0652).
  • Forgetting to interpolate. 3.5485 bar and 17.298 bar are not printed blocks; read the blocks either side and interpolate. Skipping it costs about 1 kJ/kg on h2.
  • Using the saturation row for state 1. With 10 K superheat, state 1 is at 0 °C in the superheated table (h = 253.1), not hg(−10 °C) = 246.15.
  • Using hf(45 °C) for state 3. 5 K subcooling means 40 °C liquid.
  • Rounding. 158.6/42.2 = 3.76; with unrounded values COP = 3.75. Both get full marks.

2. R22 standard VCR cycle using the exam table: 2020 2(c)

Topic A4 · 12 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

A standard VCR system developing 50 kW of refrigeration using R22 operates with a condensing temperature of 35 °C and an evaporating temperature of −10 °C. The enthalpy of the refrigerant after compression is 435.2 kJ/kg. Using the table, determine: (i) the refrigerating effect in kJ/kg, (ii) the circulation rate of refrigerant in kg/s, (iii) the power required by the compressor in kW, and (iv) COP.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

“Standard” cycle = no superheat and no subcooling. So point 1 is saturated vapour at −10 °C (on the right curve of the dome) and point 3 is saturated liquid at 35 °C (on the left curve). h2 is given, so no entropy work is needed.

PointStateCrossing ofh from
1sat. vapour, −10 °Cpe line × sat. vapour curvehg at −10 °C
2superheated vapourpc line × constant-s line through 1given 435.2
3sat. liquid, 35 °Cpc line × sat. liquid curvehf at 35 °C
4wet mixturevertical from 3 × pe lineh4 = h3

The table has no −10 °C or 35 °C row. It gives −12/−8 and 34/36 °C. Each target is exactly in the middle, so the value is just the average of the two rows (linear interpolation).

Use only the table printed with the question. The Moran table (A-7) has a different enthalpy zero and does not match the given h2 = 435.2.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: R22, Q = 50 kW, te = −10 °C, tc = 35 °C, h2 = 435.2 kJ/kg, standard cycle.

Statet (°C)h (kJ/kg)Source
1 (sat. vapour)−10(400.27 + 401.85)/2 = 401.06given table, −12 and −8 °C rows
2–435.2given
3 (sat. liquid)35(241.84 + 244.44)/2 = 243.14given table, 34 and 36 °C rows
4−10243.14h4 = h3 (throttling)

(i) RE = h1 − h4 = 401.06 − 243.14 = 157.92 kJ/kg

(ii) m = Q / RE = 50 / 157.92 = 0.3166 kg/s

(iii) w = h2 − h1 = 435.2 − 401.06 = 34.14 kJ/kg;   P = m w = 0.3166 × 34.14 = 10.81 kW

(iv) COP = RE / w = 157.92 / 34.14 = 4.63

P–h sketch checklist (draw it, 2 marks):

  1. Saturation dome; two horizontal lines: pc (top) and pe (bottom).
  2. Point 1 on the pe line, on the saturated-vapour curve (standard cycle).
  3. 1→2 along a constant-s line up to pc.
  4. Point 3 on the pc line, on the saturated-liquid curve.
  5. 3→4 vertical (h4 = h3) down to pe. Label h1, h2, h3 on the h-axis.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Using a different table. The question says “using the table”: Moran A-7 gives hf(35 °C) ≈ 87, which does not fit h2 = 435.2.
  • Swapping columns. h1 comes from the vapour column at the evaporator temperature; h3 from the liquid column at the condenser temperature.
  • Not interpolating. Taking the −12 °C row as −10 °C changes h1 by 0.8 kJ/kg.
  • Power in kJ/s. kg/s × kJ/kg = kJ/s = kW, so no extra conversion is needed.

3. Ammonia ice plant, dry saturated after compression: 2023 2(c)

Topic A11 · 12 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

An ammonia refrigerator produces 25 tonnes of ice from and at 0 °C in 24 hours. The temperature range of the compressor is from 15 °C to −5 °C. The vapour is dry saturated at the end of compression and an expansion valve is used. Assume a COP of 45% of the theoretical value. Calculate the power required to drive the compressor. Latent heat of ice is 335 kJ/kg.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

“Dry saturated at the end of compression” fixes point 2, not point 1: point 2 sits on the saturated-vapour curve at the condenser temperature. Compression is isentropic, so point 1 has the same entropy, which puts it inside the dome (wet vapour) at the evaporator temperature. That is why you find a dryness fraction x1 from entropy first.

PointStateCrossing of
2dry saturated vapour at tcpc line × saturated-vapour curve
1wet vapour at te, x1 < 1pe line × constant-s line through 2
3saturated liquid at tcpc line × saturated-liquid curve
4wet mixture at tevertical from 3 × pe line

Ice load: making ice “from and at 0 °C” needs only the latent heat (335 kJ/kg); there is no sensible part. Divide by 86 400 s to get kW.

Actual COP = given percentage × theoretical COP. Power = load / actual COP. (The interactive graph shows the theoretical power m w; divide it by the percentage to get the real answer.)

Interpolation here: Table A-13 prints 12 and 16 °C (15 °C is 3/4 of the way: fraction 0.75) and −6 and −4 °C (−5 °C is the midpoint).

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Move the sliders, press Step through to follow one process at a time, and Show table rows to read to see which rows of the tables you need. Hover over the chart to read any point.

Property data: CoolProp 8.0 grid (IIR reference), interpolated in the page; works offline.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/NH3-2023.html in a browser.

D. UNDERSTANDProperty-table rows used (how to read the table)

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: NH3, 25 t of ice per day from and at 0 °C, tc = 15 °C, te = -5 °C, dry saturated after compression, COP = 45% of theoretical, L = 335 kJ/kg.

Property (Table A-13)at 15 °Cat -5 °C
hf (kJ/kg)250.44156.86
hg (kJ/kg)1456.041436.42
sf, sg (kJ/kg K)sg = 5.14330.6248, 5.3967
15 °C = 12 + 0.75(16 − 12): interpolated between the 12 and 16 °C rows. −5 °C = average of the −6 and −4 °C rows.

State 2 is dry saturated at 15 °C: h2 = hg = 1456.04 kJ/kg, s2 = 5.1433

1→2 isentropic: s1 = s2 ⇒ x1 = (s2 − sf1)/(sg1 − sf1) = (5.1433 − 0.6248)/(5.3967 − 0.6248) = 0.9469

h1 = hf1 + x1(hg1 − hf1) = 156.86 + 0.9469(1436.42 − 156.86) = 1368.48 kJ/kg

h4 = h3 = hf(15 °C) = 250.44 kJ/kg

COPth = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1) = (1368.48 − 250.44)/(1456.04 − 1368.48) = 12.77

COPactual = 0.45 × 12.77 = 5.746

Refrigeration load Q = (ice per day × L) / seconds per day = 25 × 1000 × 335 / (24 × 3600) = 96.93 kW

Power = Q / COPactual = 96.93 / 5.746 = 16.87 kW

Sketch (T–s or P–h): point 1 inside the dome (wet, x1 ≈ 0.95), 1→2 vertical on T–s ending on the saturated-vapour curve at 15 °C, 3 on the saturated-liquid curve, 3→4 constant h.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Putting point 1 on the vapour curve. Here point 2 is dry saturated; point 1 is wet (x1 ≈ 0.95).
  • Adding sensible heat to the ice load. “From and at 0 °C” means latent heat only.
  • Applying 45% the wrong way. Actual COP is smaller than theoretical, so power is bigger: P = Q/(0.45 COPth).
  • Table zero. Other ammonia tables (e.g. the course slides) use a different zero and give h values about 1 kJ/kg different; COP and power come out the same to 3 figures (the old pack got 16.9 kW).

A. Problem

An ammonia ice plant produces 30 tonnes of ice per day from and at 0 °C. The condenser and evaporator temperatures are 20 °C and −10 °C. The vapour is dry saturated at the end of compression. The actual COP is 55% of the theoretical value. Find the power required to drive the compressor. (Latent heat of ice 335 kJ/kg.)

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

“Dry saturated at the end of compression” fixes point 2, not point 1: point 2 sits on the saturated-vapour curve at the condenser temperature. Compression is isentropic, so point 1 has the same entropy, which puts it inside the dome (wet vapour) at the evaporator temperature. That is why you find a dryness fraction x1 from entropy first.

PointStateCrossing of
2dry saturated vapour at tcpc line × saturated-vapour curve
1wet vapour at te, x1 < 1pe line × constant-s line through 2
3saturated liquid at tcpc line × saturated-liquid curve
4wet mixture at tevertical from 3 × pe line

Ice load: making ice “from and at 0 °C” needs only the latent heat (335 kJ/kg); there is no sensible part. Divide by 86 400 s to get kW.

Actual COP = given percentage × theoretical COP. Power = load / actual COP. (The interactive graph shows the theoretical power m w; divide it by the percentage to get the real answer.)

Both 20 °C and −10 °C are printed rows in Table A-13, so no interpolation is needed.

Write this in the exam

Given: NH3, 30 t of ice per day from and at 0 °C, tc = 20 °C, te = -10 °C, dry saturated after compression, COP = 55% of theoretical, L = 335 kJ/kg.

Property (Table A-13)at 20 °Cat -10 °C
hf (kJ/kg)274.26133.94
hg (kJ/kg)1459.901430.55
sf, sg (kJ/kg K)sg = 5.08490.5389, 5.4662
Both rows are printed in Table A-13.

State 2 is dry saturated at 20 °C: h2 = hg = 1459.90 kJ/kg, s2 = 5.0849

1→2 isentropic: s1 = s2 ⇒ x1 = (s2 − sf1)/(sg1 − sf1) = (5.0849 − 0.5389)/(5.4662 − 0.5389) = 0.9226

h1 = hf1 + x1(hg1 − hf1) = 133.94 + 0.9226(1430.55 − 133.94) = 1330.21 kJ/kg

h4 = h3 = hf(20 °C) = 274.26 kJ/kg

COPth = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1) = (1330.21 − 274.26)/(1459.90 − 1330.21) = 8.14

COPactual = 0.55 × 8.14 = 4.478

Refrigeration load Q = (ice per day × L) / seconds per day = 30 × 1000 × 335 / (24 × 3600) = 116.32 kW

Power = Q / COPactual = 116.32 / 4.478 = 25.97 kW

Sketch (T–s or P–h): point 1 inside the dome (wet, x1 ≈ 0.92), 1→2 vertical on T–s ending on the saturated-vapour curve at 20 °C, 3 on the saturated-liquid curve, 3→4 constant h.

For understanding – do not write
  • Putting point 1 on the vapour curve. Here point 2 is dry saturated; point 1 is wet (x1 ≈ 0.95).
  • Adding sensible heat to the ice load. “From and at 0 °C” means latent heat only.
  • Applying 45% the wrong way. Actual COP is smaller than theoretical, so power is bigger: P = Q/(0.45 COPth).

5. Refrigeration tonnage: ice and cold-storage loads (2024 1a, 2023 1d, 2020 1c)

Topic A3 · 10 + 7 + 10 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

2024 1(a): Calculate the refrigeration tonnage for 2000 kg ice melting from 0 °C to 45 °C. 2023 1(d): Calculate the refrigeration tonnage for 1500 kg ice from 0 °C to 25 °C. 2020 1(c): 600 kg of fruit enters a cold store at 25 °C and is cooled to −5 °C in 8 hours; latent heat of freezing 105 kJ/kg, specific heat 1.255 kJ/kg K. Find the plant capacity.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

1 TR (ton of refrigeration) = heat to melt 1 tonne of ice at 0 °C in 24 h ≈ 210 kJ/min = 3.5 kW.

Any load = latent part (phase change, temperature constant: m L) + sensible part (temperature change: m c ΔT). Add them, divide by the time in minutes, then divide by 210.

Ice questions with no time given are taken over 24 h (the definition of TR). Water c = 4.187 kJ/kg K, ice latent heat L = 335 kJ/kg.

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Change mass, temperatures and time; the staircase shows latent and sensible parts.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/TR.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

2024 1(a): Q = m[L + cw(t2 − 0)] = 2000[335 + 4.187 × 45] = 1,046,830 kJ per day

= 1,046,830 / 1440 = 727.0 kJ/min;   TR = 727.0 / 210 = 3.46 TR

2023 1(d): Q = 1500[335 + 4.187 × 25] = 659,512 kJ/day = 458.0 kJ/min;   TR = 2.18 TR

2020 1(c): Sensible = m c ΔT = 600 × 1.255 × (25 − (−5)) = 22,590 kJ; Latent = 600 × 105 = 63,000 kJ

Total = 85,590 kJ in 8 h = 85,590/480 = 178.3 kJ/min;   Capacity = 178.3/210 = 0.85 TR

Definition line (write it first, 1 mark): 1 TR = heat removed to freeze 1 tonne of ice from and at 0 °C in 24 h = 210 kJ/min ≈ 3.5 kW.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Forgetting the time. TR is a rate: divide by minutes (24 h = 1440 min, 8 h = 480 min).
  • Using ice c for water. Above 0 °C it is water: c = 4.187 kJ/kg K.
  • For the 2020 fruit: the paper gives one c for the whole range, so use 1.255 × 30 K. Say so in one line.

6. Aircraft simple air-cycle refrigeration: 2020 3(c)

Topic A12 · 13 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

In an aircraft refrigeration unit using the air cycle, 50 kg/min of air at 200 cm Hg gauge and 205 °C are bled off the air compressor serving the jet engine. The bled air passes through a heat exchanger leaving at 180 cm Hg gauge and 80 °C. It is then expanded through a small cooling turbine to 20 cm Hg vacuum and −10 °C. The air exhausted out of the plane is at 25 °C. Assume cp = 1.0 kJ/kg K. Determine the cooling capacity in TR and the COP based on input power to the bled-off air.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Air is the refrigerant. Hot bled air (205 °C) is cooled in the heat exchanger (80 °C), expanded in the cooling turbine to −10 °C, then sent to the cabin, where it warms up to 25 °C before leaving. That warming in the cabin is the cooling it gives.

The pressures (cm Hg) are not needed, because the temperatures at each point are given. The “input” is the energy carried by the bled air above the exhaust state: m cp(205 − 25).

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Change the turbine-exit or cabin temperature to see TR and COP move.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/AIR.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: m = 50 kg/min, cp = 1.0 kJ/kg K, bleed 205 °C, turbine exit −10 °C, cabin exhaust 25 °C.

Refrigerating effect = m cp(texhaust − tturbine) = 50 × 1.0 × (25 − (−10)) = 1,750 kJ/min

Cooling capacity = 1,750 / 210 = 8.33 TR

Input to bled air = m cp(tbleed − texhaust) = 50 × 1.0 × (205 − 25) = 9,000 kJ/min

COP = refrigerating effect / input = 1,750 / 9,000 = 0.19

Assumption stated: input energy measured from the cabin-exhaust state (25 °C).

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Using the HX exit (80 °C) in the RE. The cooling happens in the cabin, from −10 to 25 °C.
  • Converting the pressures. Not needed here: all temperatures are given.
  • Low COP is normal for air cycles (about 0.2). Do not “correct” it.

7. Summer air conditioning with ventilation air and bypass factor: 2024 5(c)

Topic B3 · 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

A refrigeration (air-conditioning) plant is shown in the figure: room sensible heat 20 kW, room latent heat 5 kW, room 25 °C DBT / 50% RH, outside air 43 °C DBT / 27.5 °C WBT, return : outside air = 3 : 1 by mass, coil ADP 12 °C, bypass factor 0.13. Determine: (i) dehumidified air quantity, (ii) sensible and latent heat gain due to outside air, (iii) total refrigeration load of the plant.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Path of the air (follow it on the chart with Step through): outside air o mixes with room return air i → mixture 1 on the straight line o–i, 1/4 of the way from i (3:1 by mass) → cooling coil pulls it toward the ADP (apparatus dew point, coil surface temperature) but 13% of the air bypasses the coil, so it leaves at 2 → supply air 2 absorbs the room heat and becomes i.

PointFound as the crossing of
iDBT 25 °C vertical × RH 50% curve
oDBT 43 °C vertical × WBT 27.5 °C sloping line
1line o–i × DBT 29.5 °C (mass-weighted)
ADPsaturation curve × 12 °C
2line 1–ADP × DBT t2 = ADP + X(t1 − ADP)

Dehumidified air = the air that goes through the coil = supply air. It must carry away the room sensible heat: ma = RSH / [cp(ti − t2)]. cpm = 1.0216 kJ/kg K is humid specific heat (1.005 + 1.88 W); many books use 1.02.

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Press Step through to follow the air from outside to the room. Hover over the chart to read DBT, RH, WBT, DPT, W, h and v anywhere.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/AC-2024.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: RSH = 20 kW, RLH = 5 kW, room 25 °C / 50%, outside 43 °C DBT / 27.5 °C WBT, 3:1, ADP = 12 °C, X = 0.13.

StateDBT °CW (g/kg)h (kJ/kg)Source
o4316.886.6psy chart; vo = 0.92 m³/kg
i259.950.3psy chart
1 (mix)0.75(25) + 0.25(43) = 29.511.6259.37mass-weighted

Mixing by mass: t1 = 0.75 ti + 0.25 to, W1 = 0.75 Wi + 0.25 Wo, h1 = 0.75 hi + 0.25 ho

Coil exit: t2 = tADP + X(t1 − tADP) = 12 + 0.13(29.5 − 12) = 14.28 °C

(i) Dehumidified air, ma = RSH / [cpm(ti − t2)] = 20 / [1.0216(25 − 14.28)] = 1.83 kg/s

Outside air, mo = 0.25 × 1.83 = 0.456 kg/s

(ii) OASH = mo cpm(to − ti) = 0.456 × 1.0216 × 18 = 8.39 kW

OALH = mo hfg(Wo − Wi) = 0.456 × 2501 × (16.8 − 9.9)/1000 = 7.88 kW

(iii) OATH = mo(ho − hi) = 0.456(86.6 − 50.3) = 16.57 kW

Total load = RSH + RLH + OATH = 20 + 5 + 16.57 = 41.6 kW = 11.8 TR

Chart sketch: mark o, i, join; 1 on it; ADP on saturation curve; line 1–ADP with 2 on it; line 2–i.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Mixing by temperature only. Mix W and h by mass; t1 by mass is fine as an approximation.
  • Taking supply air = ADP. With X = 0.13 the air leaves above ADP: t2 = ADP + X(t1 − ADP).
  • Forgetting the outside-air load. The plant must handle room load + outside air load (GTH = RTH + OATH).
  • Chart reading. Readings differ by 2–3% between charts (the older pack used Wo = 17 g/kg and got 41.8 kW). The method gets the marks.

8. Finding ADP from the room heat ratio: 2021 5(c)

Topic B3 · 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

The room sensible heat gain and latent heat gain of a conditioned space are 40 kW and 15 kW. The inside design condition is 25 °C DBT and 55% RH. The return air is mixed with outside air before entering the cooling coil in the ratio 3:1 by weight. Assuming the bypass factor of the cooling coil is 0.13, determine: (i) apparatus dew point (ADP), (ii) ventilation air in cmm, (iii) total refrigeration load of the plant. (Outside condition is not printed on some copies; taken as 35 °C DBT, 65% RH. State this.)

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Here the ADP is not given. It is fixed by the room: the supply air 2 must lie on the room line (RSHF line) through i, whose slope is set by RSH/RLH = 40/15. It must also lie on the coil line from 1 to the ADP, at the bypass position. Only one ADP satisfies both, so you try values (or use the RSHF line on the chart: draw it from i, extend it to the saturation curve… but with bypass the clean way is trial).

Tick “find ADP from RSH/RLH” in the chart below to see it solved; untick it and move the ADP slider to watch the ratio change.

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Press Step through to follow the air from outside to the room. Hover over the chart to read DBT, RH, WBT, DPT, W, h and v anywhere.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/AC-2021.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Given: RSH 40 kW, RLH 15 kW, room 25 °C / 55%, outside 35 °C / 65% (assumed), 3:1, X = 0.13.

StateDBT °CW (g/kg)h (kJ/kg)Source
o3523.395.0psy chart; vo = 0.906
i2510.952.9psy chart
1 (mix)27.514.00–mass-weighted

(i) Conditions for 2: t2 = ADP + 0.13(t1 − ADP), W2 = WADP + 0.13(W1 − WADP), and 1.0216(ti − t2) / [2501(Wi − W2)] = RSH/RLH = 2.67

Try ADP = 11.43 °C (WADP = 8.4 g/kg, psy chart): t2 = 13.52 °C, W2 = 9.13 g/kg → ratio = 1.0216(11.48) / [2501 × 0.0018] = 2.65 ≈ 2.67 ✓

ADP = 11.43 °C ≈ 11.4 °C

ma = 40 / [1.0216(25 − 13.52)] = 3.410 kg/s; mo = 0.25 ma = 0.853 kg/s

(ii) Ventilation air = mo vo × 60 = 0.853 × 0.906 × 60 = 46.3 m³/min (cmm)

(iii) OATH = mo(ho − hi) = 0.853(95.0 − 52.9) = 35.9 kW;   Total = 40 + 15 + 35.9 = 90.9 kW = 25.8 TR

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Not stating the assumed outside condition. Write it in the first line.
  • Stopping after one trial. Show one trial that works (ratio ≈ 2.67) and box the ADP.
  • cmm = cubic metres per minute: multiply m3/s by 60, and use v of outside air.

9. Ventilation rate from CO₂ balance: 2024 6(c)

Topic B5 · 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

Dhaka has twice the CO2 concentration of Khulna (400 ppm). If a classroom with 30 students is in a room of the same size in both cities, determine the required ventilation rate for each location. Also explain how to control the indoor air quality.

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

CO2 balance in steady state: CO2 brought in with fresh air + CO2 breathed out = CO2 leaving with exhaust air. So V Cout + N Np = V Cin, giving V = N Np / (Cin − Cout).

The paper gives only the outdoor ppm, so take from the class notes: Np = 0.011 cfm CO2 per seated student, allowable indoor Cin = 1000 ppm. The dirtier the outdoor air, the smaller the margin (1000 − Cout), so the more fresh air you need.

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Move the outdoor CO₂ to see why Dhaka needs 3 times the fresh air.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/CO2.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Assume (class notes): Np = 0.011 cfm CO2/person, Cin = 1000 ppm; Khulna 400 ppm, Dhaka 800 ppm.

CO2 balance: V = N Np / (Cin − Cout)

Khulna: V = 30 × 0.011 / [(1000 − 400) × 10−6] = 550 cfm = 260 L/s

Dhaka: V = 0.33 / [(1000 − 800) × 10−6] = 1650 cfm = 779 L/s (3 times Khulna)

IAQ control: (1) source control (low-VOC materials, no smoking, local exhaust); (2) filtration (MERV 8–13 for dusty Dhaka air); (3) dilution ventilation with CO2-sensor-controlled dampers; keep RH 40–60%.

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • ppm to fraction. 1 ppm = 10−6.
  • cfm to L/s: × 0.4719.
  • State the assumed Np and Cin: they are not on the paper.

Topic B8 · 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

Two of the wall faces, N and W, contain double-glazed windows (see figure). There is no heat gain through other walls. Find the required cooling capacity. Outside 43 °C DBT, 24 °C WBT; U of wall, roof, floor 1.78, 1.3, 1.2 W/m²K; ETD wall 25 °C, roof 30 °C; SHG 300 W/m², SC 0.86; lights 33 W/m² floor; 4 occupants (90 W sensible + 40 W latent each); appliances 600 W sensible + 400 W latent; infiltration 0.5 ACH. (Inside condition printed as “43 °C, 55%”: misprint, taken as 25 °C / 50%.)

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Cooling load = sum of every heat gain into the room. Two families: sensible (raises temperature) and latent (adds moisture). Each line uses one simple formula: walls and roof U A ETD (ETD = equivalent temperature difference, includes sun on the wall), glass A(U ΔT + SHG × SC), infiltration m cp ΔT and m hfg ΔW, people and appliances as given, lights W/m² × floor area.

11. Duct sizing by equal friction: 2020 6(c)

Topic B9 · 12 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

Determine the dimensions of AB, BC, CD (figure) using the equal friction method. Choose a friction rate of 0.09 mm H2O/m. Use Δpf/L = 0.002268 Q1.852/D4.973 mm H2O/m (Q in m³/s, D in m).

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Equal friction method: every section is sized for the same pressure loss per metre, f. So on the friction chart every section sits on one vertical line (f), at its own airflow Q; read the diameter there.

Step 1 is always the flows: start at the far outlets and add backwards toward the fan. Step 2 D from the chart or formula. Step 3 (if rectangular) b = 0.548 D, a = 3b for 3:1. Step 4 total friction = f × length of the longest run.

C. UNDERSTANDInteractive graph

Move the friction rate and aspect ratio; every section moves on the chart and in the table. Hover to read D and V anywhere.

Printed snapshot at the exam values. Interactive version (sliders, step-through, hover read-out): open problems/DUCT-2020.html in a browser.

F. WRITE IN EXAMModel answer

Write this in the exam

Method: equal friction, f = 0.09 mm H2O/m, D from f = 0.002268 Q1.852/D4.973.

Flows (add outlets downstream): AB = 8, BC = 6, CD = 3, BE = 2, CF = 3 m³/s

Sample: DAB = (0.002268 × 81.852 / 0.09)1/4.973 = 1.035 m

V = Q/(πD²/4) = 8/(π × 1.035²/4) = 9.51 m/s

SectionQ (m³/s)D = (0.002268 Q1.852/f)1/4.973 (m)V = Q/(πD²/4) (m/s)
AB81.0359.51
BC60.9308.84
CD30.7187.41
BE20.6186.68
CF30.7187.41

Index (longest) run = 20 + 20 + 40 = 80 m → friction loss = 80 × 0.09 = 7.20 mm H2O

G. UNDERSTANDCommon mistakes

For understanding – do not write
  • Wrong flows. A section carries the sum of all outlets downstream of it, not the outlet next to it.
  • Rectangle from area. Do not set ab = πD²/4; use the equivalent-diameter formula (same friction, not same area).
  • Units. f in mm H2O per m, Q in m³/s, D in m.

14. Duct sizing by equal friction: 2024 8(c)

Topic B9 · 15 marks · open this numerical on its own page

A. Problem

For the duct system shown in the figure, determine the dimensions of rectangular ducts with aspect ratio 3:1. Assume all dynamic loss coefficients are 0.8. (Friction rate not printed: assume 0.1 mm H2O/m and state it.)

B. UNDERSTANDHow the cycle/process works

For understanding – do not write

Equal friction method: every section is sized for the same pressure loss per metre, f. So on the friction chart every section sits on one vertical line (f), at its own airflow Q; read the diameter there.

Step 1 is always the flows: start at the far outlets and add backwards toward the fan. Step 2 D from the chart or formula. Step 3 (if rectangular) b = 0.548 D, a = 3b for 3:1. Step 4 total friction = f × length of the longest run.

Dynamic losses (bends, junctions) = K × velocity pressure pv = K ρV²/2; in mm H2O, pv = 1.2V²/(2 × 9.81). Add them along the index run to the friction loss to get fan pressure.
